sources.title: Interview — IT Administrator on Schedule Access and Staff Invites
sources.excerpt:
Objective
In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they did not think they could approve Compass AI's access to patient appointments, and both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:51-52 ). This session asked one IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices what has to happen before a new system can read a practice's appointment schedule, and who can start that. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training (in 2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 , "onboarding" means training copy for clinicians).
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an IT Administrator who handles access requests for systems used across Meridian's practices. They had not used the Compass AI practice setup flow. The researcher described steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) as the 2026-02-03 build shows them, and what the step 3 screen does and doesn't say, without sharing what other participants said. The participant did not name the scheduling system that holds the appointment schedule, and these notes don't record which system it is. This is their account of the approval process, not a review of its records.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (schedule access: privacy review) In their account, any new system that reads the appointment schedule needs a privacy review request before it is connected, and a Practice Administrator can't start one: requests are filed by IT. A practice that wants the calendar connected has to ask IT to file the request. They didn't know whether one had been filed for Compass AI.
[MEDIUM] (schedule access: still PHI) They described scheduling as the lowest-risk data on the CMIO's PHI ordering, but still PHI: the schedule carries patient names and, depending on the fields read, visit reasons. They saw this as consistent with the ordering, not a contradiction of it, because the ordering ranks the risk and doesn't remove the review.
Representative Quotes
"Lowest risk isn't no risk. It's still patient names on a schedule. It still goes through privacy review, it just shouldn't take long." — IT Administrator, P160
"A practice admin can't put in that request. They call us, we file it. If the screen just asks them to click connect, it's asking the wrong person." — IT Administrator, P160
Recommendations
On Connect calendar, route an administrator who can't approve schedule access to IT, consistent with the "Send to IT for approval" path recommended on 2026-02-03 ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:75-76 ).
Before more practices set up, confirm with IT whether a privacy review request for Compass AI reading the appointment schedule has been filed, and list the fields it covers.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Has a privacy review request for Compass AI's schedule access been filed, and which fields does it cover?
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through the setup flow's invites, or both? The participant didn't know.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: Why does the session lock recovery flow add a paused state instead of changing the idle timeout?

seeded.answer: The session lock recovery flow adds a paused state because the 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and cannot be changed [1][2][3]. IT Security confirmed this constraint during a February 17, 2026 session [1][4]. The UI change—adding an explicit “paused, draft preserved” state—is a product decision that doesn’t require altering the underlying timeout policy [1][4][3]. The contextual inquiry revealed that 4 of 5 clinicians assumed their draft was lost when the session locked, and the new state aims to address this misinterpretation without affecting the timeout itself [4][5].

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

The session lock recovery flow adds a paused state because the 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and cannot be adjusted per feature [1][2][3]. IT Security confirmed this constraint during a February 17, 2026 session [1][4]. The UI change to display a "paused, draft preserved" state is a product decision that doesn’t require altering the underlying timeout policy [1][4]. The initial contextual inquiry revealed that 4 of 5 clinicians assumed their draft was lost when the session locked, leading to re-dictation [4][5]. This behavior stemmed from the lack of clear communication about the session state, and the new paused state aims to address this by explicitly indicating that the draft is saved [4].

questions.question: Why does the confidence-highlighted draft review leave high-confidence lines unmarked?

seeded.answer: The high-confidence lines are deliberately left unmarked to encourage skimming [1][2]. The design intentionally avoids color-only signaling to meet accessibility requirements, ensuring flagged lines are distinguishable by the underline itself, not color [1]. The January 13th usability test with 6 participants (Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant) showed that 4 of them were able to skim high-confidence lines for the first time, indicating the confidence indicator was successful in changing reviewing behavior [3]. This supports the synthesis finding that visible uncertainty, rather than raw accuracy, is the key to changing how clinicians review notes [2]. The design team was looking for a “trust-building lever” since September, and the usability test suggests the confidence indicator is that lever [3].

sources.title: Confidence-Highlighted Draft Review — Hi-Fi Mockup (GA Candidate)

Researcher: Priya Patel

[LOW] (confidence indicator (positive)) The new per-line confidence highlighting (low-confidence transcription shown in a subtle underline) was well received and, notably, 4 of 6 participants said it let them skim high-confidence lines for the first time across the whole testing history — the first session where reduced line-by-line reading was observed.
